kind.note: Named as the officers' quarters by Hubbard in 1827, by Andreas's summary of the rebuilt fort, and by the 1855 photograph key.

construction.note: Hubbard, standing in the fort in 1827: 'The old officers' quarters built of logs on the west'. The 1855 key says 'wood', which is the same claim less precisely. A CORRECTION TO THIS PROJECT'S OWN DOSSIER: docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 1.2 reads Andreas as giving brick officers' quarters on the west and flags a conflict with the 1855 key. Andreas's page 84 states no material for them at all, and his page 264 - Hubbard's own words - says logs. The conflict was a misreading; the two sources agree.

period_brick.note: T-3387: laid in K03's hand-made garrison brick (data/components/prairie_1904/k03_face_brick.json `soft_mud_red_garrison`): a soft, sand-struck, clamp-burnt red in wide lime joints, its colour the sheet's brick row (a shade darker), in the bonded K03 panel the 1904 walls wear, each brick shuffled. That this is brick is the record's construction and the archetype's stack argument; that it was a hand-made soft-mud brick of this colour and bond is the reconstruction (L-k03-period-brick-3387).

stories.note: RECONSTRUCTED STILL, BUT NO LONGER 'NOT ATTESTED ANYWHERE' (T-3124). That phrase was stale. Hubbard, describing the fort as he first saw it in October 1818, says 'The officers' quarters were outside of the pickets, fronting east on the parade, and was a two-story building of hewn logs' (hubbard_autobiography_1911, leaf 74, printed p. 36, committed text lines 2353-2358). That is earlier evidence for two storeys than anything this note used to rest on. IT DOES NOT PROMOTE THE GRADE, for two reasons the same book supplies. First, Hubbard contradicts himself on where the building stood: page 36 puts the officers' quarters OUTSIDE the pickets, while his 1827 walk round the fort puts 'The old officers' quarters, built of logs, on the west, and within the pickets' (hubbard_autobiography_1911, leaf 205, printed p. 167, committed text lines 7612-7613), which is where the 1830 plan draws this range; the source record lists the contradiction as something it does not supply. Second, nothing says the two-storey building of 1818 is the same range that stood in July 1835 rather than an earlier one — the post stood ungarrisoned from October 1823 to October 1828 and again from May 1831 to June 1832 (Hubbard's own table, printed p. 35), and no building inside it is dated. So the 1818 sentence is carried forward only CONDITIONALLY, on the reading that p. 36's 'outside' is a slip and the range never changed. The count's older argument still stands beside it: this range and the commandant's quarters are the two buildings the 1855 photograph shows as 'the principal buildings of the Fort', and a single-storey log range would not read as one of two principal buildings beside a two-storey brick one. That photograph is a diagnostic only, twenty years after the scene date, and no camera has been solved on it as a matched view of July 1835.

wall_height_m.note: No height is attested. 4.8 m is two storeys of log wall at period course counts. The number inherits the storey count's weakness above it.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal form for a log range of this period and plan.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for any building in this fort. 34 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a shingled or riven-shake roof of this period and span, and it is inferred from construction practice rather than measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested. A 60 ft officers' range through Chicago winters needs a stack at each end by type. The COUNT is the inference; position, size and material are the archetype's, per docs/LIBERTIES.md.

gallery.note: AN UPPER PIAZZA, BUILT AS A RECONSTRUCTION ON HUBBARD'S EARLIER TEXT, NOT AS ATTESTATION (T-3124). Hubbard, of the officers' quarters he saw in 1818: 'A piazza extended along the entire front on a line with the floor of the second story, and was reached by stairs on the outside' (hubbard_autobiography_1911, leaf 74, printed p. 36, committed text lines 2353-2358). It is rendered with the fort archetype's existing two-level gallery (gallery_storeys 2): an open ground level of posts under an upper walk at the second floor, a rail along its front, and a canopy from the main eave. THE GRADE STAYS RECONSTRUCTED because the same unresolved questions the storey count carries apply here with more force: Hubbard puts that building OUTSIDE the pickets on p. 36 and the log officers' quarters WITHIN them on the west on p. 167, and nothing identifies the 1818 building with this 1835 range, so the piazza's continuity into the 1831-1835 garrison is conditional on both. THE PRIOR REFUSAL IS KEPT ON THE RECORD: until T-3124 this attribute read false with the note that nothing said the 1816 fort's ranges had galleries, that Whistler's 1808 'Galliaries fronting the parade' belonged to the first fort, and that John H. Kinzie called the two forts 'differently constructed'. That was written without p. 36, and it is the alternative a visitor would have seen had the text not been read. EVERY DIMENSION IS RECONSTRUCTED: the 2.1 m reach, post sections and rhythm, deck, rail, pales and canopy fall are the helper's choices (docs/LIBERTIES.md L-first-fort-double-galleries and L-second-fort-officers-piazza-3124); Hubbard gives none. THE OUTSIDE STAIRS ARE NOW MODELLED (T-2388): the occurrence is Hubbard’s; the right-end side, straight run, width, risers and rails are reconstructed under gallery_stair_side. The prior refusal because their location was unrecorded is superseded by that explicit bounded choice. The 1855 photograph is diagnostic only and is not a matched July 1835 view.

gallery_storeys.note: Two levels because Hubbard puts the piazza 'on a line with the floor of the second story' (hubbard_autobiography_1911, leaf 74, printed p. 36, committed text lines 2353-2358), so the walk is the upper one and the ground level under it is open. Graded reconstructed, not inferred, because the identification of Hubbard's building with this range is unresolved (see gallery and stories). The upper floor sits at the existing 2.4 m storey line of the unchanged 4.8 m wall; the helper's other dimensions are reconstructed.

face_openings.note: THE OLD LAYOUT, WRITTEN DOWN, NOT A NEW READING (T-3124). These are exactly the rectangles the archetype's procedural default already built on this range — five bays to the parade front with the ground-floor centre bay given to a door, four to the back, each storey's sills at 0.30 and heads at 0.72 of its 2.4 m — declared explicitly so that the upper piazza's supports can be set clear of them. Nothing moves: every opening stands where it stood before, and the left and right gable ends keep no openings, as before. No picture or text gives this building's openings; Hubbard's room list (kitchen, dining and store rooms below, one large room above) is not a fenestration, and every rectangle remains reconstructed.

gallery_stair_side.note: OUTSIDE ACCESS COMPLETED AS A BOUNDED RECONSTRUCTION (T-2388). Hubbard, printed p.36 (leaf74, text2353-2358), says the upper piazza was reached by stairs on the outside. This supplies the occurrence in1818, carried conditionally to1July1835 under the existing gallery continuity interpretation; it gives no side, run, width, material or rail. We choose one straight timber flight continuing from the right (south) end of the existing upper walk, entirely outside the wall: 1.0m clear width, 3.6m run to its existing2.4m floor,14risers of171mm,70mm treads, two stringers and0.95m handrails. The gallery end rail opens only at this access; the wall and its openings remain unchanged. Exact geometry and side are liberties, not historical measurements. This explicitly supersedes gallery.note’s prior refusal to model any stair merely because its location was unknown. It does not identify either unnamed stair/galleried range in the1893 retrospective with these quarters.

function.note: Quarters for the post's subordinate officers. In 1827, with the fort ungarrisoned, Hubbard found them occupied by Russel E. Heacock 'and one other American family' - which is evidence about 1827, not about 1835.

occupants.value: Assistant Surgeon Philip Maxwell and Lieut. James Allen, and the rest of the post's subordinate officers unnamed
occupants.note: NAMED, NOT PROMOTED (T-1348). This block read 'subordinate officers of the garrison' and claimed the same thing it claims now; what it did not do was say who. Two men in this dataset are commissioned officers of the United States Army printed at Chicago across 1 July 1835. Philip Maxwell is Andreas's assistant surgeon, on duty at the post from 3 February 1833 to the abandonment, and hh_maxwell_philip already carries this building as its lives_at. James Allen is the papers': army officer and engineer, printed at the Democrat of 25 March 1834 and of 13 August 1834 and at the American of 18 July 1835 — seventeen days after the scene date, which is what makes his household present rather than uncertain. NO SOURCE PUTS EITHER MAN IN THIS BUILDING, so the grade does not move: the Army quartered a lieutenant and a post surgeon in the subordinate officers' quarters and this dataset holds one. ELEVEN OTHER NAMES WERE RULED OUT, each for a stated clause — a militia colonel, a man on the town poll roll, a soldier's trade read once in January 1834 and never again. The whole adjudication is docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn_garrison_1835.md. The enlisted strength stays unwritten and unnumbered here (T-1349), and Hubbard's 1827 civilian tenants belong to the years when there were no troops.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by John Baptist Baubian, 28 May 1835
land_owner.note: THE UNITED STATES RESERVATION. This is the same tract L108 already derives for `1835_no_build_ground.json` — from G1, Madison's line and the traced waterline — so the polygon is inherited rather than built again, and `check.sh` already re-derives it. The register's own row is the second, independent witness to the date L108 quotes from Andreas: Beaubien's pre-emption, 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene date. The derived polygon is short of the documented 75.69 acres for the reasons L108 states, and is a floor rather than the reservation. WHETHER THE ENTRY HELD IS NOT READ HERE: it was disputed, and this row records the entry the register carries and nothing about its outcome. THE MARGIN IS ONLY 26 m, which is inside the working horizontal uncertainty of the georeference (about 20 m) doubled, so the grade drops a tier: the tract is right if the constructed line is, and nothing here proves the line to better than that. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

placement.position_note: READ OFF THE 1830 HARRISON PLAN. Position in pixels on the plate Andreas reproduces at vol. 1 p. 113, scaled at 1.10 ft per pixel (the scale derivation is on fort_dearborn_palisade and in docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md section 3), rotated to the sheet's true-north arrow, and hung on the fort centre at local E +1152, N +221. Carry +/-20 percent on the offset from the fort centre and +/-20 m on the fort itself. The facade bearing is the fort's 8-degree rotation plus the side of the parade this building faces, because every range in this fort fronts the parade. Hubbard, 1827: 'The old officers' quarters built of logs on the west, and within the pickets'. Andreas: 'The officers' quarters were on the west side'. The 1830 plan draws a long range against the west wall, and that range is this building.
placement.symbolic_location: Inside the west wall of Fort Dearborn, fronting east onto the parade.

grade.why: Known from maps or written records; no picture of it has been found.

footprint.note: TWO READINGS THAT DO NOT AGREE, AND THIS RECORD TAKES THE STATED ONE. The 1855 key gives 'the Officers' Quarters, B (wood, about 30x60 ft,)' - 9.14 x 18.29 m, which is the polygon here. The 1830 plan draws the west range about 30 ft deep and about 80 ft long at the scale this project derives, so the two agree on the depth to within 3 percent and disagree on the length by nearly 40 percent. THE STATED FIGURE WINS, and the reasoning is worth writing down because it decides several records: the scale that would overrule it was itself calibrated on the other stated figure in the same caption, so using it to correct that caption's second number is close to circular. What that costs is legible - the modelled building is about 6 m shorter than the plan draws its range - and it is why this footprint is inferred while the commandant's is documented. If the 1830 plan is right the officers were housed in an 80 ft range; if the 1855 caption is right they were in a 60 ft one; nothing reached settles it.

construction.note: NOT STATED BY EITHER WITNESS, and the two available readings pull opposite ways, so this records the weaker claim rather than the more interesting one. FOR LOG: every building inside this fort that this dataset grades at all is log by the same argument as the barracks, the garrison built with what it cut, and a barn is the last building on a post to get sawn stuff. AGAINST LOG: a cupola is a finished carpenter's detail and sits more naturally on a framed barn. Log is taken because it is the local convention and the smaller claim; the cupola is recorded on its own attribute and argues with this one in the open.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the type for a barn of this span, and it is what a cupola needs a ridge for.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for any building at this fort. 34 degrees is the figure every other Fort Dearborn record here carries, taken from the archetype's mid-range for a riven-shake roof of this period and span, and it is inferred from construction practice rather than measured off anything.

wall_height_m.note: No height attested. About thirteen feet to the eave: a barn that takes a loaded hay wagon through its door and carries a loft over it, and the archetype's own size-aware default for a 14.4 x 9.4 m footprint is 3.5 m, so this is half a metre above the convention rather than an invention away from it.

door.note: Not attested. A barn serving a four-acre field and a garrison's teams is a building a loaded wagon drives into, which is what the archetype's `wagon` door is for. A man door on it would be the larger claim.

door_side.note: The long wall the plate draws facing south-east, toward the garrison garden and the fort's own ground rather than toward the river bank behind it. The archetype's front faces the bearing `rotation_deg` names.

loft.note: Nobody says this barn had a loft. It is the convention for the type — hay goes over the floor a wagon uses — and it is graded as the invention it is. What a visitor sees of it is the pitching door in the gable.

paint.note: Not stated. Unpainted is the archetype's own default and the treatment of every working building in this town; paint on a military barn would be the claim.

cupola.note: OCCURRENCE STATED, BOUNDED FORM NOW BUILT (T-2388). Harrison’s plan literally labels Big Barn with Cupola, so this attests the occurrence under the existing plan/1835 continuity interpretation. This descriptive boolean remains record_only; the actually consumed cupola_shape and three explicit metric attributes now build it. The prior refusal to add any cupola solely because size, glazing, louvres and position were unknown is superseded: we choose one plain boarded square body with a pyramid cap at the existing ridge midpoint, without glazing, louvres or finial. Shape, position, material and every dimension are reconstructed, not measured from the plan or from an unidentified panorama building. This is the separately named barn cupola, not another version of the already-delivered blockhouse cupola.

cupola_shape.note: Plain boarded square body under a pyramid cap, centred on the existing gable ridge. No picture identifies this barn’s cupola; shape, midpoint placement, unpainted boards and lack of openings/finial are a bounded reconstruction of the source’s one word, not an image measurement.

cupola_width_m.note: A1.2m square body: about one eighth of the9.4m roof span, enough to read as a small barn ventilator without dominating the47ft barn. Exact width is a liberty, not attested.

cupola_body_height_m.note: The body eave1.0m above the existing ridge, with its bottom seated0.08m below the main roof at the side edges to avoid floating gaps. Both height and joint are reconstructed.

cupola_roof_rise_m.note: The pyramid cap rises0.45m above the body eave. The pitch, cap reach and joinery are reconstructed; the label supplies no detail.

function.note: Hubbard calls it 'the military barn' in so many words; the plan calls it the Big Barn with Cupola and draws it inside the fort's fenced ground beside the Cultivated Field belonging to The Fort. What was kept in it is not stated and is not inferred here: a barn on a post of this date held forage, teams and the field's implements, but which of those is a guess and the record claims the building, not its contents.

placement.position_note:
TWO WITNESSES PUT THIS BARN IN THE SAME PLACE, TWICE, AND THAT IS WHY IT IS INFERRED RATHER THAN CONJECTURAL. The plate names it — Big Barn with Cupola, lettered beside a drawn building west-south-west of the fort — and Gurdon Hubbard, describing the same ground from memory of the late 1820s, writes: 'West, and a little south, of the fort was the military barn, adjoining which, on the east, was the fort garden, of about four acres' (hubbard_autobiography_1911, leaf 75, printed p. 37, committed text lines 2392-2399). THE SECOND CLAUSE IS THE CHECK, and it is a strong one: the fort garden is already committed, independently, as fort_dearborn_garrison_garden. Its polygon's nearest corner stands 36.4 m from the position this record derives, and the garden lies east and a little south of the barn — which is Hubbard's sentence, in coordinates neither he nor this record's derivation had sight of. Nothing was moved to make that come out.

READ OFF THE 1830 HARRISON PLAN, BY THE SAME RULE AS THE ELEVEN RECORDS ALREADY TAKEN FROM IT. Internet Archive leaf n242 of historyofchicago01andr (Andreas vol. 1, p. 113), rotated 90 degrees anticlockwise so the sheet's own true-north arrow stands vertical, is 2715 x 2003 px. On that image the stockade's ink runs from x 1356 to x 1535 and from y 553 to y 730, so the enclosure's centre is pixel (1445, 644); the committed palisade record hangs that centre on local E +1152, N +221, which is UTM 448224.70 E, 4637616.80 N. Pixels convert at 1.10 ft/px (0.33528 m/px), the scale docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md section 3 derives from the commandant's quarters. THE ANCHOR AND THE SCALE ARE CHECKED, NOT ASSUMED, and the check is the garrison garden — the one thing on this plate that is both drawn and already committed. Its committed centre lands at pixel (1209, 1008) under this transform; the drawn diamond's centre measures (1207, 1002). Seven pixels, 2.3 m. A second check runs the other way: the committed blockhouse centre predicts pixel (1385, 698) and the drawn blockhouse square measures (1375, 710), 16 px or 5.4 m. WHAT THE TRANSFORM CANNOT DO is beat its own inputs. The enclosure measures 180 px across at this scale, which is 60 m against the committed palisade's 53 m — a 13 % spread, inside the +/-20 % the scale carries, and the reason is visible on the plate: 180 px is the OUTER edge of an engraved line four to six pixels thick. So carry +/-20 % on this offset from the fort centre and +/-20 m on the fort itself, exactly as every plate-derived record here does.

THE PIXEL. The drawn barn is a hatched parallelogram whose four corners measure (1118, 872), (1140, 892), (1110, 925) and (1088, 905), centre (1114.0, 898.5) — 331 px west and 254.5 px south of the fort centre, which is 111.0 m west and 85.3 m south of it.

IT IS NOT BEAUBIEN'S BARN, and the question is worth answering because the two stand 50 m apart, which is inside the error either carries. data/structures/beaubien_barn.json is the old cabin Jean Baptiste Beaubien had lived in before 1817 and afterwards used as a barn, placed by eye inside his own group on Block 5; this is the garrison's barn, drawn on a military plan inside the fort's fenced ground and called 'the military barn' by a man who walked through it. Different owner, different evidence, different enclosure. They are not distinguishable by distance and they do not need to be.
placement.symbolic_location: West and a little south of Fort Dearborn, outside the pickets in the fort's own outer enclosure, with the garrison garden adjoining it on the east.

grade.why: Known from maps or written records; no picture of it has been found.

footprint.note: NO SOURCE GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION. 14.4 x 9.4 m is about 47 x 31 ft, measured across the ink centreline of the drawn parallelogram — 43 x 28 px — at the derived 1.10 ft/px. Read it at +/-20 %, so somewhere between 38 x 25 and 56 x 37 ft. The long axis is the front, and it runs at bearing 42 degrees as drawn. WHAT SUPPORTS THE SIZE beyond the pixels is the plate's own adjective: it is the only building on this sheet the draughtsman troubled to call BIG, and 47 ft of barn is big for this town in 1830 without being improbable for a garrison that kept teams, forage and the four-acre field Hubbard describes south of it.

wall_kind.note: Juliette Kinzie, inside it in 1831: 'The fort was inclosed by high pickets, with bastions at the alternate angles.' Andreas: 'a square stockade'. A picket line - upright posts set in the ground - is what both describe, and it is the one thing about this wall that two sources state rather than imply.

construction.note: Not stated. 'Pickets' in this literature means split or roughly squared timber posts set upright, and the fort was built by soldiers out of local timber. The archetype builds squared posts, which is the commonest form and the one that matches the hewn work in the town across the river. THE HEAD OF THE POST IS OURS, AND IT NOW HAS AN ATTRIBUTE OF ITS OWN - see picket_head_m, which carries the number and its own reconstructed chip (T-0094, T-0200; docs/LIBERTIES.md L179). Every picket is sharpened over its top 0.312 m - 8.4 percent of the 3.7 m height, and CUT OUT OF that height rather than added to it, so the wall is not made taller by its own points; a visitor at the north wall reads the sawtooth, which is the whole reason the archetype does it, because a flat-topped post reads as a fence rail and a pointed one as a stockade. NOTHING REACHED DESCRIBES THE HEAD OF A FORT DEARBORN PICKET, and the plate said to draw them pointed does not. Measured on p4_0, the coloured view from across the river: the curtain's top is a RULED LINE, straight to 0.45 px rms over 138 resolved columns, while the same plate resolves individual pickets at a 10 px pitch and stands the curtain 43 px tall - so a head of this proportion would have serrated that top by 3.6 px, eight times the residual, and the draughtsman drew none. p4_1 rules the same flat cap. That refutes 'the plate draws them pointed' without settling the head either way, so the point remains a reconstruction and remains declared. tools/measure_picket_plate.py holds the property and prints the whole reading.

picket_height_m.note: THE SOURCE GIVES AN ADJECTIVE AND THIS RECORD NEEDS A NUMBER. Kinzie says 'high pickets' and nobody else says anything at all. 3.7 m is twelve feet, the common height for a frontier stockade of this class, and it is a guess dressed in a plausible number. A visitor looking at the height of this wall is looking at our arithmetic, not at evidence.

picket_width_m.note: Unattested. Roughly a ten-inch face, which is what a split oak or cedar picket of that height needs to stand without racking. IT MOVES WITH picket_spacing_m OR NOT AT ALL, because what a wall reads as is the ratio between the two and neither means anything alone - T-0185 asked whether the pair should be coarsened to the proportion p4_0 draws, and the reasoning that kept them is written out on picket_spacing_m rather than twice. In short: at the plate's own scale this face is 2.78 px wide and the gap beside it 0.70 px, under the 2 px the plate's finest stroke work can hold, so the plate could not have drawn this wall whatever the fort was made of. docs/LIBERTIES.md L47.

picket_spacing_m.note: Unattested. Set so the posts stand shoulder to shoulder with the narrow gap a hand-set picket line actually leaves, rather than touching perfectly, which reads as a fence panel. THE ONLY PICTURE ANYONE HAS OF THIS FORT DISAGREES, AND T-0185 IS WHY IT DOES NOT MOVE THIS NUMBER. p4_0 resolves separate posts at a 10 px rhythm on a curtain 42.9 px tall - 0.23 of the wall's height per post, which on a 3.7 m wall is an 0.86 m post nobody ever split, and nearly three times coarser than the 0.081 this record builds. That disagreement was measured rather than argued about (tools/measure_picket_plate.py). At the plate's own scale of 11.6 px per metre, THIS wall's rhythm would be 2.78 px of post and 0.70 px of GAP - and the narrowest gap that plate holds anywhere on the same curtain is 2 px, 2.9 times wider. The draughtsman drew the finest picket line his medium could carry. His pitch is a reading of the lithograph and not of the fort, so it is not evidence about 1816 and cannot be adopted. THE OTHER HALF IS ABOUT THE MODEL AND IS WHY THE FINE RHYTHM IS KEPT: tools/measure_picket_reading.mjs finds the wall resolving as separate posts at every stand a visitor can reach - a 34 px rhythm at the north gate on a desktop, 16 px on a phone, and 4 px against an expected 4.49 px from p4_0's own stand across the river. It falls under the pixel grid at exactly one place, a phone at that river stand, where a 1.62 px pitch beats into a 4 px moire; that is the same bind the draughtsman was in and T-0266 owns it. A drawing has one viewing distance and a walkable reconstruction has all of them, so the two cannot be held to one rhythm. This number answers to the near one, which is the only one a visitor can choose. docs/LIBERTIES.md L47.

picket_head_m.note: HOW MUCH OF EACH POST IS THE SHARPENED HEAD, AND IT IS OURS - NOTHING REACHED DESCRIBES THE HEAD OF A FORT DEARBORN PICKET. 0.312 m is 8.4 percent of the 3.7 m height and is CUT OUT OF that height rather than added to it, so the wall is not made taller by its own points. WHY THE NUMBER IS THIS NUMBER: one picket width and a bit (0.24 x 1.3), which is the proportion a splitting axe leaves on a post of this section, held under a ceiling of 18 percent of the height so a short picket cannot become a spike. That is a drawing argument and not a claim about 1816 - a flat-topped post reads as a fence rail and a pointed one reads as a stockade, and the sawtooth is what makes a visitor at the north wall see a fort rather than a paddock. THE PLATE SAID TO DRAW THEM POINTED DOES NOT: p4_0 rules the curtain's cap straight to 0.45 px rms over 138 resolved columns while resolving individual pickets at a 10 px pitch on a 43 px wall, so a head of this proportion would have serrated that line by 3.6 px, eight times the residual; p4_1 rules the same flat cap. That refutes 'the plate draws them pointed' without settling the head either way, so the head stays a reconstruction (T-0094). THIS VALUE WAS A PYTHON EXPRESSION UNTIL T-0200. It lived in PalisadeParams.picket_point_m, where the confidence model could not grade it and the popup could not show it; it is stated here at the tier it earns, at the identical number the expression produced, so no vertex moved when it was declared - the rebaked master is byte-for-byte the file that stood before. The archetype still derives the head for any palisade record that does not state one. docs/LIBERTIES.md L179.

gate_sides.note: Two independent statements. Kinzie: 'Large gates opened to the north and south.' Andreas: 'It had two gates, one on the north and the other on the south side.' The 1830 plan draws a break in each of those two walls and in neither of the others, and Hubbard's 1827 account places buildings by reference to both - 'the store-house and guard-house were on either side of the southern gate; the sutler's store was east of the north gate'. Three sources, one arrangement. T-2388: two smaller side posterns are now a bounded reconstruction of Kinzie’s distinct additional clause, not two more large gates. Her actual paragraph reads: Large gates opened to the north and south, and there were small posterns here and there for the accommodation of the inmates. The two main gates retain their attested sides and existing3.6m width; the additional east/west sides and count of two are reconstructed, with separate gate_overrides.

gate_width_m.note: 'Large gates' is the whole attestation. 3.6 m is twelve feet, wide enough for a loaded team, which is what a fort gate has to pass. The leaves are built shut; nothing says how they hung or which way they swung.

bastion_corners.note: Andreas, of the rebuilt fort: 'was defended by bastions at the northwest and southeast angles. The block-house was in the southwest corner.' Kinzie, independently: 'bastions at the alternate angles'. Hubbard in 1827: 'the block-house was located at the southwest and the bastion at the northwest corners'. The 1830 plan draws a work at exactly three angles and leaves the north-east plain. GUARD: the widely repeated 'two blockhouses, one on the south-east corner, the other at the north-west' belongs to the FIRST fort - the passage it comes from ends 'Such was the old Fort previous to 1812' - and applying it here is the commonest error about this building.

bastion_length_m.note: Unattested. The 1830 plan draws the corner works as shallow rectangular projections; this is that shape at a size the plate supports to about +/-40 percent, which is worse than the enclosure's own error bar because the works are small on the plate.

bastion_projection_m.note: Unattested. How far the work stands proud of the curtain, read off the same small marks on the same plate.

posterns.note: OCCURRENCE DESCRIBED, ACTUAL OPENINGS NOW DRIVEN BY gate_sides/gate_overrides (T-2388). Kinzie1831 explicitly contrasts large north/south gates with small posterns here and there for accommodation of the inmates. The old refusal to model any postern solely because locations were unknown is superseded by two reconstructed side wicket seats. This descriptive boolean does not itself drive geometry; the consumed gate controls build and the actual fort-gates renderer hangs their leaves. Counttwo, east/west side, offsets,1.5m width and leaf detail are reconstructed; no picture has been assigned an exact postern.

gate_overrides.note: TWO SMALL SIDE POSTERNS, NOT AN ADDITIONAL PAIR OF LARGE GATES (T-2388). Actual Wau-Bun ch.XVII paragraph independently reread10November2026 at the existing source URL: Large gates opened to the north and south, and there were small posterns here and there for the accommodation of the inmates. The conjunction distinguishes small additional openings; the plural does not give a count, side, metric size, exact place or carpentry. Two is the minimum plural and our bounded choice. Each is1.5m wide, the supported narrow wicket kit: one at east-wall localv41.0m (offset+14.5), in the gap between barracks and sutler, and one at west-wall localv11.5m (offset-15), between blockhouse and officers’ range. Both use one inward-swinging paling leaf at existing wall height, safely shut initially. The south/north main gates, their3.6m spans and positions stay unchanged. These seats, width, leaf construction, same-height head and swing are reconstructed liberties rather than mapped postern marks. They avoid occupied building footprints and do not borrow the first fort’s separately attested west wicket.

function.note: The enceinte of a garrisoned United States infantry post. Occupied on the scene date - see the structure-level occupants block and docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md section 2.

occupants.value: United States 5th Infantry, Maj. John Greene commanding
occupants.note: THE FORT WAS OCCUPIED ON 1835-07-01 AND THIS PROJECT CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED IT. Andreas gives the sequence: the garrison was withdrawn in 1823, the post was re-garrisoned in October 1828, the troops were removed to Green Bay in May 1831, and 'In June [1832] the fort was once more garrisoned. Major William Whistler being assigned to the command' - held continuously from then until 29 December 1836. For the scene date itself Andreas brackets the command rather than naming it: DeLafayette Wilcox 'commanded until December 18, 1833, and again from September 16, 1835', with 'Major John Bender, Major John Greene and Captain and Brevet-Major Joseph Plympton ... in command at various times' between. The drloihjournal chronology fills the bracket with Maj. John Greene, 5th Infantry, 18 December 1833 to 16 September 1835, which is unfootnoted but lands exactly inside Andreas's two dates. STRENGTH IS NOT ATTESTED for mid-1835; Andreas gives two companies of infantry in 1833 and nothing later, so no number is recorded here. The garrison is why the gates are built shut rather than open and why the fort is modelled maintained rather than decaying.

placement.position_note: PLACED FROM THE ONLY PLAN OF THIS FORT ANYONE HAS FOUND. F. Harrison Jr.'s 1830 survey of the mouth of the Chicago River, drawn for the harbour works and reproduced by Andreas at vol. 1 p. 113, draws Fort Dearborn IN PLAN: a quadrangular picket enclosure with a work at three of its four angles, four ranges set against the walls, two small buildings flanking a break in the south wall, and a larger block outside the south-west angle. Positions in this record were read off that plate in pixels, scaled at 1.10 ft per pixel of the archive.org page image, rotated to the sheet's own true-north arrow, and hung on the fort centre at local E +1152, N +221 - the Wright 1834 reading that docs/ROADMAP.md S5a records as cross-checked to 35 m against the modern successor landmark. THE SCALE IS THE WEAK LINK AND IT IS STATED RATHER THAN BURIED: the sheet carries no scale bar, so 1.10 ft/px comes from setting the north range equal to the commandant's quarters at 'about 25x50 ft' in the key to the 1855 photograph, and it is checked by the gap between the west and east ranges coming out 71 ft against that key's 80 ft parade width. Carry +/-20 percent on every dimension derived this way, on top of the +/-20 m the datum already carries. THE ARRANGEMENT IS BETTER EVIDENCE THAN THE SCALE, and it is corroborated: Gurdon S. Hubbard, describing the inside of this fort in 1827 (Andreas I, p. 264), names the same buildings on the same sides in the same relation to the same two gates. An 1830 engineer's plan and an 1827 eyewitness agreeing building by building is what licenses inferred here rather than conjectural. See docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md sections 3 and 4. THE ROTATION IS READ OFF THE SAME PLATE and is the least expected number in this record: the fort's walls are drawn about 8 degrees clockwise of true north, measured as the mean of all four walls against the sheet's own north arrow, which sits within 0.2 degrees of vertical once the leaf is rotated. Eight degrees is inside what a woodcut re-engraving can invent, so it is inferred and not documented - but the fort sat on a river bank inside a bend and had no grid to align to, and a square post whose walls all lean the same way by the same amount is more likely to be a fort that was not square with the meridian than an engraver who tilted four lines consistently.
placement.symbolic_location: The south bank of the Chicago River inside the bend, on the Fort Dearborn Reservation at the river mouth; the site of the modern Michigan Avenue bridge's south approach.

grade.why: Known from maps or written records; no picture of it has been found.

footprint.note: A SQUARE OF ABOUT 53 m (174 ft), AND EVERY PART OF THAT SENTENCE HAS A DIFFERENT WARRANT. That it was SQUARE is Andreas in terms: 'The fort, as rebuilt, consisted of a square stockade inclosing barracks, quarters for the officers, magazine and provision-store' - and the 1830 plan agrees, drawing the two wall-to-wall distances within 3 percent of each other (161 and 157 pixels). THE SIZE IS DERIVED, NOT STATED. No source reached gives a dimension of this stockade; Quaife, who wrote the standing monograph on the fort and had the War Department files, prints Captain Whistler's measured 1808 draught of the FIRST fort and states no dimension of the second one anywhere. So 53 m is the 1830 plan measured at the scale that record's position note derives, and it carries +/-20 percent - the fort is somewhere between about 140 and 210 ft on a side. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: the polygon is a rectangle because the plan draws a quadrangle, and nothing attests the corners were true or the sides equal to the foot.

kind.note: Named by Andreas and by Hubbard, both at the south-west angle. GUARD: the widely repeated 'two blockhouses, one on the south-east corner, the other at the north-west' is the FIRST fort - its source passage ends 'Such was the old Fort previous to 1812'. This fort has one blockhouse and two bastions, and the bastions belong to fort_dearborn_palisade.

construction.note: Not stated for this fort. The 1803 War Department instruction for posts of this class required 'the block-houses to be constructed of timber, slightly hewed', which is the type; nothing says the 1816 rebuild departed from it.

stories.note: Not stated. Two storeys with the upper one jettied is what makes a blockhouse a blockhouse: the 1803 instruction says the block-houses are 'so placed as to scour from the upper and lower stories the whole of the lines', which is a two-storey building described by what it does.

wall_height_m.note: Unattested. Two storeys of hewn log. A guess in a plausible range.

upper_overhang_m.note: Unattested at this fort. The jetty of the upper storey over the lower is the defining feature of the type and it is invented here at a typical size; a visitor looking at the overhang is looking at a definition, not at evidence.

loopholes.note: Unattested at this fort. The 1803 instruction for this class of post describes blockhouses scouring the lines from both storeys and barracks with port-holes 'for the use of musketry', so loopholes are what the building is for - but that is a specification for the first fort and the pattern, spacing and height of every slit built here is ours.

roof_type.note: Unattested in words. A four-sided pitched cap over a near-square plan is the surviving type. Andreas's own 1808 index for the FIRST fort notes 'the Cupolas are not yet built on the Block Houses as laid down', which attests a cupola on that fort's blockhouses and says nothing about this one; the cupola this record now carries is read off this fort's own pictures instead, and stands in `cupola` with its own confidence rather than being folded into this attribute.

roof_pitch_deg.note: Unattested. A shallower pitch than the ranges because a pyramid over a wide plan gets tall fast.

chimneys.note: RECONSTRUCTED AT NONE, AND THAT IS A CHOICE ABOUT WHAT TO DEPICT, NOT A FINDING ABOUT HEATING (T-2388). This record used to count one stack — 'a blockhouse manned in a Chicago winter is heated' — and the archetype stands a single stack at the exact centre of the plan, which is where this fort's own pictures put a cupola instead. Panel 5 of the Kurz & Allison sheet and the two Wau-Bun reproductions of the 1831 view all draw the small square cupola on this roof and none of them draws a stack beside it, so the invented stack was both unattested and in the way of a pictured feature, and the pictured feature wins. WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM: that the blockhouse was unheated, that it had no flue, or that nothing ever stood on this roof besides the cupola. Pictorial sources are tier 5 and their silence is not testimony; the 1856 Kellogg/Blanchard print (filed, misleadingly, as `chicago_fort_dearborn_river_mouth_1830.jpg`) depicts about 1836-1849 and does show a small ambiguous projection beside a louvred cap, and that later detail is left unresolved rather than backdated onto 1 July 1835. The count is recorded at 0 because nothing reached counts one, and a stack has not been quietly moved somewhere else to keep it.

cupola.note: PICTURED, AND ONLY PICTURED (T-2388). Panel 5 of the Kurz & Allison sheet, captioned 'Fort Dearborn as rebuilt 1835', draws this blockhouse with a small square body at the centre of its four-sided cap, under a little four-sided cap of its own; the two Wau-Bun reproductions of the 1831 view draw the same body. Two independent-looking depictions of this fort's blockhouse agree on the feature, which is what carries INFERRED rather than attested: the sheet is an 1893 retrospective, it is tier 5, it dates several of its own subjects wrongly, and its caption is not proof that this feature stood on 1 July 1835. EVERY DIMENSION IS RECONSTRUCTED and none of it is in this record: the side, the height, the cap's pitch, the plain boarded sides and the absence of louvres are the archetype's working reconstruction at the proportions the panel shows, and docs/LIBERTIES.md owns them. The louvres and the ambiguous secondary projection of the 1856 Kellogg/Blanchard print are NOT built: that print depicts about 1836-1849.

function.note: The fort's one blockhouse, at the south-west angle, flanking the south and west curtains. It outlived the fort as a landmark: Wentworth records that when the reservation was sold in 1839 'the land whereon the block-house stood ... was not parted with'.

The 1830 plan draws a heavy hollow block at the south-west angle, projecting outside the curtain on both faces - the only element of the fort drawn that way. placement.symbolic_location: At the south-west angle of Fort Dearborn, standing astride the corner of the stockade and projecting outside it.

grade.why: Pictured: 7 of the pictures on the Images tab show it.

footprint.note: MEASURED, AND LARGER THAN A BLOCKHOUSE OUGHT TO BE. 14.52 x 9.80 m is about 48 x 32 ft, read off the 1830 plan at the derived scale after correcting for the fort's rotation. A period blockhouse is usually 20 to 30 ft square, so this is either an unusually large one or - more likely - the plate drawing the blockhouse together with the return of the curtain round it as a single heavy block. The measurement is recorded rather than quietly shrunk to the expected size, because shrinking it would be substituting a typology for the only plan that exists. Carry +/-25 percent and read the note.

kind.note: Hubbard 1827 has the commanding officers living in it; the 1855 key names it the Commandant's Quarters. Andreas's summary of the rebuilt fort lists 'quarters for the officers' among what the stockade enclosed.

construction.note: Two independent statements twenty-eight years apart. Hubbard, 1827: 'the brick building, just within the north stockade'. The 1855 key: '(brick, about 25x50 ft.)'. THIS MATTERS BEYOND THIS BUILDING: docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 11 says there was 'no brick building of consequence yet on the south side' in 1835 and excepts the fort - correctly, and this is the building it means.

period_brick.note: T-3387: laid in K03's hand-made garrison brick (data/components/prairie_1904/k03_face_brick.json `soft_mud_red_garrison`): a soft, sand-struck, clamp-burnt red in wide lime joints, its colour the sheet's brick row (a shade darker), in the bonded K03 panel the 1904 walls wear, each brick shuffled. That this is brick is the record's construction and the archetype's stack argument; that it was a hand-made soft-mud brick of this colour and bond is the reconstruction (L-k03-period-brick-3387).

stories.note: Not stated. A 50 x 25 ft brick building housing the commanding officer of a two-company post, standing tall enough to be one of the 'two of the principal buildings of the Fort' identified in a photograph taken from across the river, is two storeys by type. The inference is from the building's size and its prominence, not from a statement.

wall_height_m.note: No height is attested for any building in this fort. 5.4 m is two storeys at about nine feet of interior height each plus floor structure, which is the ordinary figure for officers' quarters of this class. What is inferred is that the wall falls in this range, not that it is exactly 5.4 m.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for a rectangular range of this period, and it is what the building silhouetted in the 1855 photograph reads as. Inferred from type.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for any building in this fort. 34 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a shingled or riven-shake roof of this period and span, and it is inferred from construction practice rather than measured.

chimneys.note: The 1855 caption mentions the building's chimneys in passing while locating the ferry landing - 'under the west chimney of the Commandant's quarters' - which attests at least two by implying a west one and an east one. Two is the ordinary number for a double-pile range of this size in any case. WHERE they stood, how big they were and what they were made of are the archetype's, which is the standing admission in docs/LIBERTIES.md.

paint.note: Bare brick. Nothing says this building was rendered, painted or whitewashed; the whitewash in the sources belongs to the board fence of the 1850s compound and to John H. Kinzie's boyhood memory of the FIRST fort's blockhouses.

gallery.note: A PLAIN FRONT DOUBLE GALLERY, ADOPTED FOR JULY 1835 AS A BOUNDED CONTINUITY CHOICE (T-2388). The actual public-domain 1881 contained cut after Alexander Hesler’s 1855 photograph, with its explicit printed p.93 key, securely identifies this brick range as Commandant’s Quarters A and shows two gallery levels along its parade front. That strongest named picture governs the broad form; it does NOT date the gallery’s construction or prove it was unchanged in 1835. The existing interpretation identifies this with the brick commanding-officer range Hubbard describes inside the north stockade in 1827 and Harrison draws in 1830, under the fort’s 1816 rebuilding range. A front piazza is compatible with that retained fabric and arrangement; Hubbard’s distinct 1818 officers’ quarters already had an upper piazza, so the form is possible at this post before the scene date. That analogy supports plausibility, not identity or independent attestation of this gallery. We fairly choose continuity of the pictured plain gallery into 1 July 1835 rather than invent an alteration date. The occurrence IN THIS SCENE, every dimension, plain posts, deck, rails and canopy remain reconstructed. Existing full front width 15.24m, reach 2.1m, upper walk at the unchanged 2.7m storey line, 0.14m posts/deck and 0.95m rail are the existing gallery kit’s bounded choices. Footprint, surveyed placement, bearing188degrees, walls, roof, stacks and openings stay as before. No wraparound corner connection, additional stairs, unidentified 1850 soldiers’ gallery, paint or elaborate joinery is copied backwards.

gallery_storeys.note: Two levels follow the securely named 1855 A view: an open lower post level and an upper walk at the second floor. Carrying that arrangement into July1835 is the explicit reconstructed continuity choice in gallery, not an attested installation date. The existing5.4m wall and2.7m storey line stay fixed; exact deck, rail, pale rhythm, canopy fall and support sections remain liberties.

face_openings.note: The unchanged procedural layout written explicitly only so the existing gallery support solver clears every sash, casing and sill horn (T-2388). Captured directly from this range’s prior builder: four windows on each front storey, three on each rear storey, and one centred ground-floor front door; gable ends remain unread/empty as before. Every rectangle, sill, head, width and position is identical to the former default. Neither the 1855 picture nor an unkeyed earlier range is used to attest these counts or dimensions. The gallery’s original even support grid would intersect window trim; the existing explicit-opening API moves only its new supports onto solid piers.

placement.symbolic_location: Inside the north wall of Fort Dearborn, west of the north gate, fronting south onto the parade.

grade.why: Pictured: a picture on the Images tab shows it.

footprint.note: THE ONLY BUILDING IN THIS FORT WHOSE SIZE A SOURCE STATES. The key to Alexander Hesler's 1855 photograph, printed in Wentworth's 1881 address: 'the Commandant's Quarters, A (brick, about 25x50 ft.)'. 25 x 50 ft is 7.62 x 15.24 m, recorded converted with the original figures stated, per data/datum.json's units rule. IT IS ALSO THE CALIBRATION FOR EVERY OTHER DIMENSION IN THIS COMPLEX, which is worth stating plainly because it makes one number load-bearing far beyond its own building: the 1830 plan draws this range 48 pixels long, and setting 48 px = 50 ft is where the 1.10 ft/px scale comes from. The check that the calibration is not circular is the plate's own aspect - the drawn range is 1.9 times as long as it is deep against the key's stated 2.0 - and the parade width falling out at 71 ft against the same key's 80. THE DATE IS THE WEAKNESS: 'about 25x50' is a caption to a photograph taken twenty years after the scene date, and it is graded documented because it is a stated measurement of this building, not because 1855 is close to 1835.

stories.note: 'a two-story frame building' (DRLOIH), and chicagology's witnesses use the second floor throughout — 'a stairway in this hall led to the second floor'.

construction.note: DISPUTED, AND THE DISPUTE HAS A NAME ATTACHED TO IT. Two sources call the Green Tree a two-storey frame building outright. Against that, chicagology's Town of Chicago page reports that W. H. Stow — the man who built the Western Hotel two blocks south — 'did claim that the Green Tree was originally of logs and it was not until years afterward that it was covered with weatherboarding and given the appearance of a frame building.' Frame is adopted because it is the reading of both detailed accounts and because the interior the witnesses describe is a framed interior: board partitions, a stair hall, whitewashed plank walls, chambers laid out on a 12 ft module. The log-core claim is one man's recollection, recorded second-hand, about a rival's house, and it is carried in this record as log_core so it is not lost. Braced versus balloon is separately unattested: balloon framing appeared in Chicago in 1832-33, so an 1833 building could be either, and braced_frame is the conservative reading for the earlier date.

log_core.note: Records the rejected reading so it stays visible. W. H. Stow claimed the Green Tree was originally of logs and weatherboarded only years later. Adopted as false for the reasons in the construction note; if it is true, the 1835 building is a weatherboarded log structure rather than a frame one, which changes the wall section but not the massing, the plan or the placement.

cladding.note: Not directly attested for this building. Clapboard is the standard cladding for a frame building of this type and period, and the competing log-core account calls the covering 'weatherboarding', which is the same thing under another name — so both readings of the construction converge on a lapped horizontal board exterior.

paint.note: A CORRECTION TO A CLAIM IN CIRCULATION. The Green Tree is sometimes described as whitewashed, including in this project's own research summary, but the attested whitewash is INTERIOR: Edwin Gale writes that 'The walls, ceilings, and board partitions had evidently received a coat of whitewash when the house was built'. Nothing describes the exterior finish. Unpainted weathered clapboard is the reading adopted, and it is positively supported by the Sauganash's white paint being remarkable at Wolf Point in 1831 — if the Green Tree had been painted white two years later, the contrast the sources draw would be weaker. Not attested either way; the c. 1859 photograph would settle it.

wall_height_m.note: THE BEST-FOUNDED WALL HEIGHT IN THE DATASET, because a ceiling height is actually attested: 'Seven and one-half feet is rather low for a hotel ceiling.' Two storeys at 7 1/2 ft = 15 ft, plus floor structure between them and a sill course, gives about 16 1/2 ft = 5.0 m to the plate. The 7 1/2 ft is documented; the allowance for joists and sill is the inference.

roof_type.note: John Gray: 'There should also be a small attic window in the gable end, for we used the attic, too.' A gable end with a window in it is a direct attestation of the roof form — one of the few in this dataset that is not typological. With the front on Canal and the long side on Lake, the gable ends face east and west and the ridge runs east-west along Lake Street.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 38 degrees is mid-range for period gable framing and leaves an attic tall enough to lodge people in, which the sources say it did.

fenestration.note: The PANE CHARACTER is attested — a guest chamber 'about 12x12, with two windows 6x8', small-paned sash, plus 'a small attic window in the gable end'. Two windows per 12 ft chamber on a 40 x 25 ft two-storey block implies a regularly fenestrated elevation. Since T-0083 the ARRANGEMENT is carried by elevation_scheme, read off plate '11'; this value still states the pane character, which the plate agrees with — 6-over-6 sash in even bays.

That later recollection may describe a changed or schematic form, but it does not date the door to 1 July 1835, and the drawings do not prove its historical absence on that date. The choice follows the two pictured opening patterns as inferred form; exact July-1835 appearance remains uncertain. The original undated Andreas plate is not dated by the local reproduction's 1838 caption, and Trowbridge is retrospective, not an independent contemporary 1835 survey. THE LOW ADDITION, BUILT AT THE REAR AND DECLARED. That asymmetry is itself evidence worth recording: a west wing fits the ground only under the 'Lake and West Water' placement reading the position note carries as this record's largest residual uncertainty. If that reading ever wins, the second wing goes up with the move. The wing the views draw beside masts is consistent with either.

gallery.note: NO EVIDENCE EITHER WAY, and unlike the Sauganash there is no retrospective depiction in the project's hands to reason from. placement.position_note:
RE-SEATED 2026-10-22 ON THE OWNER'S REPORT (T-3029): 5.80 m WEST, the northing and bearing unchanged. The owner, in the 1835 scene: "green tree tavern in 1835 is sunken, it needs to be on the ground". It was: the renderer beds a building on the lowest ground under it, and the T-0141 seat below was measured on the footprint polygon alone, while the rear ell (form.rear_ell, built since T-0083 off the east gable) runs 4.5 m further down the bank, its far corner 1.54 m from the traced waterline. Bedded to the ell's foot, the inn stood 0.58 m under its own front door; bedded to its bounding box, as the renderer then did, 0.88 m. The rule is the T-0141 rule with the whole building in it: walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, this is the first seat at which every wall foot the mesh puts on the ground, ell included, meets the modelled ground within 0.10 m, the relief 95% of the 1835 town's structures stand on. Here it is 0.099 m, and the ell's far corner stands 4.59 m from the bank. The move is inside the 20 m working uncertainty below and argues nothing new about the corner: the source still puts the inn at Lake and West Water, and the bank still decides how close to it the inn can come. The paragraphs below are the T-0141 seat as it was measured, kept as the reading this one corrects.

MOVED 2026-09-24 ON THE OWNER'S RULING OF 2026-09-21 (T-0141): from the north-east corner of Lake and Canal to the north-east corner of Lake and West Water, 116.40 m east, measured between the old east face and the new one. The northing did not change at all. THE MOVE IS ARGUED FROM THE SOURCE AND NOT FROM A PICTURE'S FRAMING. DRLOIH's article on this tavern gives the corner as 'Lake and West Water Streets'; West Water was the street that ran along the west bank while Canal lay a full plat module further west, and the owner ruled that statement preferred over the same article's gloss 'now Canal Street'. The ship masts that read beside and beyond the inn rather than above its own roofline from the `green_tree` stand (T-0122, T-0140) are the SYMPTOM that sent somebody to look at the placement; they are not a reason to move a building.

WHAT THE OLD PLACEMENT WAS, because a committed building that moves without its previous reading surviving is a town quietly rewriting itself. PLACED 2026-08-09 at EPSG:26916 E 446937.4, N 4637299.6, facade bearing 270: the west face on Canal Street's east frontage and the south face on Lake's north frontage, each half an 80 ft platted street from the modern Lake-and-Canal intersection centre read from OpenStreetMap (E 446913.0, N 4637287.4). That reading rested on chicagology's 'Northeast Corner of Lake and Canal Streets' and on DRLOIH's own body text, 'the N.E. corner of what is now Lake and Canal Streets' — both name Canal in modern terms and one says 'what is now', which is why Canal was adopted at the time. The residual was recorded then and is the thing the ruling settled: modern Canal at Lake stands about 146 m back from the modern west-bank line, so the two readings are a full plat module apart. The check that would settle it from paper is still the lot geometry on Wright 1834 or Hathaway 1834, which nobody has read.

HOW THE NEW COORDINATE IS ARRIVED AT — two constraints, one of them recomputed by tools/validate.py. (1) NORTH OF LAKE, unchanged: the south face stands 12.192 m north of the Lake-and-Canal control's northing, half the 80 ft platted module, which is the `platted_corner` derivation below and keeps the building out of Lake's platted corridor. (2) THE RIVER END: the footprint's north-east corner stands 3.01 m from the 1834 traced west bank of the South Branch (data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut/river.geojson) — 5.71 m measured due east at that corner's own northing — and the standoff is the MODELLED GROUND'S OWN LIMIT rather than a chosen setback. The bank falls away toward the water, and a 12.19 m sill plate cannot sit level across that fall: seated hard on the bank the footprint's perimeter stands 0.88 m off the terrain beneath it, which is a building arriving nowhere and would owe a liberty. Walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, the first seat whose whole perimeter comes within the walker's 0.35 m step-up of the modelled ground is this one, at 0.294 m, with the footprint dry at all 425 samples of a 24-by-16 grid over it. So the tavern comes forward to the bank as far as the committed ground carries it, which is what 'forward to the bank' can mean here. Facade bearing is UNCHANGED at 270, due west onto West Water: F. H. Taylor's 'The fornt was on Canal street and this side was on Lake' is a claim about the street the front faced, and on the ruling's reading that street is West Water; the long elevation still runs east-west along Lake, and John Gray's second entrance is still 'on the Lake street front about the middle of the long side'. Working uncertainty about 20 m, which is the georeference's and the traced bank's and not an additional guess.

WHAT THE MOVE DISPLACED, AND ON WHOSE RULE. The committed `west_water` centreline ran through this footprint. T-0768 carried the bank offset 37.12 m past the Wolf Point turn under a stated rule — carry it until the riverward corridor reaches a committed footprint that stands ACROSS the roadway rather than beside it, and cut the line there — and the Green Tree is now the first such footprint, its nearest corner 3.01 m from the bank and its furthest 15.90 m, so it stands across the roadway exactly as James Kinzie's house does. So the line is cut at local [-20.32, -98.49]: 22.53 m shorter, ending 2.30 m south of Lake's own north platted kerb. The owner's ruling anticipated a collision and named T-0251 to settle it — the loser re-seated on its own evidence before it is withdrawn — and this line's own evidence is the rule above. The cost is written where the street is, in data/streets/1835.json: Fergus 1839's 'W. Water st north of West Lake st' again attests a street this reconstruction gives no modelled length north of Lake. Nothing already placed was displaced; the nearest committed footprint is James Kinzie's house, whose nearest corner stands 9.14 m north-west of this one.

AND THE PLATE'S COMPOSITION NOW READS, which is what T-0122 asked for and what the old placement could not give. Plate "11" of the 2026-08-11 prefire views hangs ship masts over this tavern's roofline; from the old stand the nearest water on that bearing was 157 m out and a 14.5 m mast on a 1.1 m deck needed to be inside 83 m, so the masts read beside and beyond the inn instead. The schooner moored in the reach below the forks (data/boats/era_boats.json, boat_schooner_wolf_point_2, whose own note already called this reach 'the one open water on the Green Tree Tavern's own eastward sight line') now lies 29.16 m beyond the ridge. The ridge stands 7.98 m above the building's base — 5.0 m of wall and a 38 degree gable over a 7.62 m width — which is 8.96 m on the committed heightfield, and the masthead is 15.6 m above the water. A viewer has to stand at least 0.93 of the ridge-to-mast distance back from the ridge before the masthead clears it, so the `green_tree` stand moved with the building, to Lake Street's own south platted frontage 34.85 m from the ridge on the schooner's bearing (local [-44.11, -121.52], yaw 33.3). The masthead reads 1.44 m above the roofline there, and between 1.36 m and 1.52 m for an eye anywhere from 1.6 m to 1.8 m. From the old standoff — 12.2 m off the front wall — it still does not clear, and that is geometry rather than a placement question: an 8 m ridge seen from 12 m subtends more than a 15.6 m masthead seen from 41 m, wherever the building stands.

footprint.note:
DERIVED FROM THE ATTESTED INTERIOR, not invented and not measured. This is the only footprint in the parcel with a textual basis. The bar-room occupied one whole end, which is consistent. WHAT IS ATTESTED IS THE MODULE, NOT THE COUNT: no source gives the building's overall length or width, and a plan with three rooms rather than two on one side would make it about 52 ft. Treat the length as plus or minus about 20 per cent and the depth as firmer. The polygon is the two-storey core only — the 'low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left' that John Gray recalls is NOT included, because its size is unattested and its date is unknown. The c. 1859 photograph (chm_green_tree_1859) would settle the overall dimensions from the proportions of a known-height building; it has not been seen.
